messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 38

Mateo has spent forty years measuring his life in counts and rhythms. At sixty-two, he still moves through his neighborhood the way he used to move through a choreography: weight grounded, eyes forward, shoulders rolling with the invisible music only he can hear. He and his wife, Elena, have shared a life built on the discipline of the studio and the warmth of shared meals where Spanish and English weave together over the table. Nine months ago, the metronome stops. The collision occurs on a Tuesday. Rain has turned the intersection into a mirror, and a delivery truck crosses the solid line. He watches the glass bloom across his windshield, feels the airbag’s violent crack against his sternum, endures the sudden, brutal compression of his ribs. He walks away. The driver of the other car does not. From that morning forward, the street becomes a grid of threats. What begins as hesitation behind the wheel quickly becomes a full-body recalibration. When Elena drives, Mateo sits in the passenger seat with his knees pressed together, his gaze fixed on the tires rather than the road. He calculates trajectories before the light turns, his breath catching in short, shallow pulls every time a vehicle slows too abruptly. At night, the intersection returns. The dreams do not evolve; they repeat the same second over and over—the screech of rubber, the sickening pivot, the impossible geometry of metal folding inward. He wakes with his hands clenched, jaw tight, already bracing for an impact that has long since passed. Dance was never just his profession; it was his native tongue. He built his career on spatial precision, on the trust of shared weight, on knowing exactly where his body ends and another’s begins. Now, when he steps into the studio to guide a rehearsal, his own frame feels like borrowed armor. During a recent master class, he leads a younger partner through a slow sequence, but each time she shifts her weight against him, his trapezius muscles spike, his breath hitches, and his eyes lock onto the floorboards. He counts the measures until the music dissolves, waiting for the studio walls to give way. He has not stepped onto a stage in six months. The proscenium arch now looks less like an entrance than a threshold he cannot cross. In our sessions, Mateo speaks with careful precision, his fingers tracing the grain of the armrest as if anchoring himself to solid ground. He describes how his nervous system still holds the collision like a live wire. He apologizes to doorframes when he brushes past them. He avoids side streets, takes detours without telling himself why, and catches himself mapping emergency exits every time he enters a crowded café. The question that circles his thoughts most often is not what happened, but why he remains. He carries the faces of the truck driver’s family, whom he meets briefly at the hospital, and he wonders how they learn to walk through the world again without counting the seconds. He still loves the music, but he listens through closed car windows now, the glass a barrier that keeps the rhythm at a safe distance. He tells me yesterday that he is trying to relearn how to occupy his own skin. The city still turns, still breathes, still moves to its own steady pace. He is learning to stand inside the silence between beats without flinching.
